rows.name: context-16-frozen-16
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: A timeout doesn’t mean the charge failed—it may have succeeded while the response was lost. Reusing the same durable idempotency key lets the server recognize the retry and return the original outcome, while an atomic claim on that key prevents concurrent duplicate execution. For a local charge, the charge and its durable outcome record must commit atomically; for an external payment provider, a local database transaction alone is insufficient—the provider must support idempotency with the same stable key, or an equivalent deduplication mechanism.

review.note: Timeout may follow committed charge. Stable durable key/atomic claim deduplicates; local outcome/charge atomic, external provider idempotency separately required.
review.usefulPrefix: A timeout doesn’t mean the charge failed—it may have succeeded while the response was lost. Reusing the same durable idempotency key lets the server recognize the retry and return the original outcome, while an atomic claim on that key prevents concurrent duplicate execution.

rows.name: context-21-frozen-21
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Because compare-and-swap applies your update only if the value still matches your expectation. If you expected 5 but another thread changed it to 7, retry expecting 7 and recompute the increment as 8; keeping expectation 5 can repeatedly fail, while proposing 6 would overwrite progress if accepted. A weak compare-and-swap can also fail spuriously, so use the returned observed value even when it is unchanged.

review.note: Actual frozen CAS5->observed7 requires expectation7/proposal8, notstale6. Weak spurious failure qualifier present; no invented original numbers.
review.usefulPrefix: Because compare-and-swap applies your update only if the value still matches your expectation. If you expected 5 but another thread changed it to 7, retry expecting 7 and recompute the increment as 8; keeping expectation 5 can repeatedly fail, while proposing 6 would overwrite progress if accepted.

rows.name: context-27-frozen-27
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: A circular buffer is a good fit because it provides FIFO push and pop in constant time with exactly 17 storage slots. Tracking the number of stored items distinguishes empty from full, so all 17 slots are usable and an overflow push can fail without changing the queue. The tests verify empty-pop failure, overflow rejection, FIFO order, and correct reuse of slots when the indices wrap around.

rows.name: context-30-frozen-30
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it does not make concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time. Starting with Alice and Bob both on call, each transaction reads that snapshot, checks that the other person remains on call, and updates only its own row to go off call. Under snapshot isolation, the writes do not conflict, so both can commit, leaving nobody on call. In a serial execution, the second transaction would see the first person already off call and fail its check—that is why this outcome is not serializable.

review.note: Atomicity !=serial order; both Alice/Bobold-on snapshots plus disjoint own-off writes allowzero, while serialsecondguard rejects removal.
review.usefulPrefix: Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it does not make concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time.
